headline: Sleeping in on weekends may lower blood pressure risk

sources.title: 'People should not feel guilty': weekend lie-in may be good for you, experts say (The Guardian)
Sleeping in on weekends is good for the heart: What research has shown (Al Jazeera)
Weekend Catch-Up Sleep Lowers Blood Pressure Risk, Korean Study Finds (Seoul Economic Daily)
Protective role of weekend catch-up sleep on hypertension in adults with physical inactivity (ESC 365, European Society of Cardiology)

chunks.text: For years, sleep experts have warned people not to {{sleep in}} on weekends. Extra weekend sleep, they said, can {{throw off}} the body's [[internal clock]]. Now a study presented at the European Society of Cardiology [[congress]] in Munich, Germany, on August 29, 2026, suggests that people who {{catch up on}} lost sleep [[in moderation]] have lower [[odds]] of high blood pressure. Newspapers worldwide reported the finding within days.

verbs.correct: To sleep later than usual in the morning
verbs.wrong: To spend the night at a friend's home
verbs.why: Many people sleep in on their day off, and a teenager will sleep in until noon if nobody wakes him. For years, sleep experts have warned people not to sleep in on weekends.

verbs.correct: To disturb the normal working of something
verbs.wrong: To delay something until a later time
verbs.why: A long flight can throw off your sense of time, and one wrong number can throw off a whole calculation. Experts said that extra weekend sleep can throw off the body's internal clock.

verbs.correct: To do something you missed earlier
verbs.wrong: To become popular among many people
verbs.why: After a vacation you catch up on your email, and a student who was sick catches up on the lessons she missed. The study suggests that people who catch up on lost sleep in moderation have lower odds of high blood pressure.

chunks.text: The Korea University researcher who presented the study {{went through}} data from a national [[health survey]] of 40,727 South Korean adults from 2016 to 2023. Catch-up sleep was the difference between weekend and weekday [[sleep duration]]. Weekend catch-up sleep was linked to 6 percent lower odds of high blood pressure. The benefit {{went up}} to 6.9 percent among [[physically inactive]] adults. The [[ideal]] amount {{came to}} 1 hour 27 minutes, with 9 percent lower odds.

verbs.why: An accountant goes through the receipts at the end of the month, and a teacher goes through every essay before giving grades. The Korea University researcher went through data from a national health survey of 40,727 South Korean adults.
Rent goes up almost every year, and the temperature goes up quickly after sunrise. The benefit went up to 6.9 percent among adults who were physically inactive.
The bill came to 40 dollars, and the total number of visitors came to just over a thousand. The ideal amount of extra weekend sleep came to 1 hour 27 minutes.

chunks.text: Blood pressure normally {{goes down}} during sleep, but too little sleep can reduce that [[nightly drop]], said a sleep scientist at the University of Utah. The researcher said a [[lack of sleep]] keeps the heart and [[blood vessels]] working harder, and weekend sleep may help the body [[recover]]. But she {{pointed out}} that more is not always better. People who slept more than four extra hours had a higher risk, because an [[irregular schedule]] may {{cancel out}} the benefit.

verbs.why: Prices go down after the holidays, and the water level goes down during a dry summer. Blood pressure normally goes down during sleep, but too little sleep can reduce that nightly drop.

verbs.correct: To tell people about a fact
verbs.why: A tour guide points out that the market is closed on Mondays, and a friend points out that your bus leaves from a different stop today. The researcher pointed out that more sleep is not always better.

verbs.correct: To remove the effect of something
verbs.wrong: To measure the effect of something
verbs.why: A big dessert can cancel out the benefit of a workout, and a late fee can cancel out a small discount. The researcher said an irregular schedule may cancel out the benefit of catch-up sleep.

chunks.text: Experts still advise people to {{stick to}} a regular [[bedtime]] and [[wake-up time]]. A cardiologist at the British Heart Foundation, who was not involved in the study, said many people {{miss out on}} sleep because of work and family [[commitments]]. The study is not a [[green light]] to {{cut back on}} exercise, the cardiologist said, but people need not feel [[guilty]] about sleeping late on weekends. The researcher agreed: extra sleep may simply be the body's way of {{making up for}} lost sleep.

verbs.correct: To keep following a plan or routine
verbs.wrong: To be easy to notice among others
verbs.why: It is hard to stick to a diet during the holidays, and a good driver sticks to the speed limit. Experts still advise people to stick to a regular bedtime and wake-up time.

verbs.correct: To fail to get something good
verbs.why: If you arrive late, you miss out on the best seats, and people who never travel miss out on a lot. A cardiologist at the British Heart Foundation said many people miss out on sleep because of work and family commitments.

verbs.wrong: To stop the supply of something
verbs.why: The doctor told him to cut back on salt, and the company cut back on travel to save money. The cardiologist said the study is not a green light to cut back on exercise.

verbs.correct: To replace something that was lost
verbs.wrong: To invent a story that is not true
verbs.why: A big dinner makes up for a missed lunch, and a summer class can make up for the weeks a student lost while sick. The researcher said extra weekend sleep may simply be the body's way of making up for lost sleep.

mainIdea.s: A large South Korean study linked a moderate amount of extra weekend sleep to lower odds of high blood pressure. Sleeping more than four extra hours, however, was tied to a higher risk.
mainIdea.why: About 90 minutes of extra weekend sleep was linked to 9 percent lower odds, while people who slept more than four extra hours had a higher risk.

mainIdea.s: Researchers found that the more extra sleep people got on weekends, the less likely they were to have high blood pressure. Experts now say a regular bedtime no longer matters for the heart.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the benefit stopped at a moderate amount, and people who slept more than four extra hours had a higher risk. Experts still advise a regular bedtime.

mainIdea.s: A survey of shift workers found that people who sleep during the day have higher blood pressure than day workers. Doctors say night shifts should be limited to protect the heart of every worker.
mainIdea.why: The study looked at extra weekend sleep among adults in general, not at shift workers or daytime sleep.

lines.text: Did you see the study about sleeping late on weekends? It might actually be good for your blood pressure.
Really? I thought the experts said you should never {{sleep in}}.
They did. The worry was that it would {{throw off}} your internal clock. But this new study says a little extra sleep, in moderation, is fine.
The ideal amount {{came to}} 1 hour 27 minutes. People who got about that much had 9 percent lower odds of high blood pressure.
[[Guilty as charged]]. I do at least that every Saturday.
Then [[that's a relief]]. A researcher at Korea University {{went through}} a survey of more than 40,000 adults over seven years.
Blood pressure normally {{goes down}} while you sleep. If you {{miss out on}} sleep all week, that nightly drop gets smaller.
Makes sense. And the weekend is when you {{catch up on}} it.
Right. But the researcher {{pointed out}} that more is not always better. Past four extra hours, the risk actually {{went up}}.
Exactly. An irregular schedule can {{cancel out}} the benefit. [[Within reason]], though, you're fine.
I still think I should {{stick to}} a regular bedtime.
[[Easier said than done]]. And it's not a reason to {{cut back on}} exercise, either. One heart expert was very clear about that.
Fair. So a little extra sleep is just the body {{making up for}} lost sleep.
That's how the researcher put it. Nothing to feel guilty about.
